content.text: Result submitted.

data.verdict: The fragment job is not 'lost', 'hung on a swallowed START', or 'missing a DONE IRQ': it is still on the GPU, blocked behind a page-table translation fault (READ, 0x0b2aa000) that the driver never resolves. kbase in exactly this situation either grows/backs the region and replays the access (growable-tmem fault path) or kills the job and resets; our port's MMU IRQ handler only logs and clears the latch, so the requesting core (the tiler, which is also the fragment-job executor - it never goes idle) stalls forever, JS_STATUS stays ACTIVE(0x08), and neither DONE nor ERR is ever posted. The secondary structural bug that keeps it stuck across recoveries: recovery stops the slot through JS_COMMAND_NEXT (0x60) instead of the current-job JSn_COMMAND (0x20), so the wedged job is never actually stopped.

answers.1_submit_sequence: EQUIVALENT. Vendor kbase_job_hw_submit writes HEAD_NEXT_LO/HI (mali_kbase_jm.c:72-73), AFFINITY_NEXT_LO/HI (:101-102), CONFIG_NEXT (:105-119) then COMMAND_NEXT=START (:146); cfg = as_nr | END_FLUSH_CLEAN_INVALIDATE(3<<12) | START_MMU(1<<10) | START_FLUSH_CLEAN_INVALIDATE(3<<8) | THREAD_PRI(8) = 0x83700|as_nr. Ours: panfrost7580_job.c:702-720 (HEAD, AFF, CONFIG from p7580_js_config(), panfrost7580_jm_hw.h:173-180 = same 0x83700|as_nr), wmb() at :747, COMMAND_NEXT=START at :748. Differences: (a) our extra wmb() - harmless/stronger; (b) the vendor honours JSn_CONFIG_JOB_CHAIN_FLAG only under BASE_HW_FEATURE_JOBCHAIN_DISAMBIGUATION (t72x does not have it - not in base_hwconfig.h:525-539), while our chain_mode knob (:718) ORs the bit when desc[4]&1, i.e. from the job_descriptor_size bit - wrong source, but chain_mode=0 by default; (c) the vendor asserts kbasep_jm_is_js_free() i.e. COMMAND_NEXT==0 (mali_kbase_jm.h:47-53), we WARN_ON the same (panfrost7580_job.c:677). Nothing here can explain the hang; HEAD==TAIL==jc and JS_STATUS=ACTIVE prove the START was consumed and the descriptor fetched.
answers.2_completion: OUR HANDLER DOES NOT LOSE A DONE. Vendor: kbase_job_irq_handler reads the MASKED JOB_IRQ_STATUS and returns IRQ_NONE when 0 (mali_kbase_core_linux.c:1039-1048), then kbase_job_done(kbdev,val) (mali_kbase_jm.c:280-435) walks bits, reads JSn_STATUS only for failed slots (:337-340), writes JOB_IRQ_CLEAR with that slot's two bits (:346), reads JOB_IRQ_JS_STATE (:347), logic for 'no active jobs left' re-checks RAWSTAT (:373), re-reads RAWSTAT into done at the tail (:408) and loops; JOB_IRQ_MASK is permanently 0xFFFFFFFF (mali_kbase_pm_driver.c:601). Ours: panfrost7580_job.c:815-935 reads STAT and RAWSTAT, ORs them, per-slot CLEAR of (1<<j)|(1<<(j+16)) (:847), handles DONE (:857-930) and ERR (:967-1035). JOB_INT_MASK is (js_present|js_present<<16) (:580), identical coverage. Two benign deltas: we clear before reading JSn_STATUS (:847 vs :852) - JS_STATUS is not cleared by JOB_IRQ_CLEAR; and we snapshot once instead of re-reading RAWSTAT - the line is level-driven, so re-entry covers it. Decisive: a dropped/masked DONE leaves RAWSTAT latched (that is exactly what the hang_inject knob simulates, :687-697); RAWSTAT=STAT=0 at timeout proves the JM never posted DONE for slot 0. kbase's only missing-interrupt workaround (BASE_HW_ISSUE_10883, mali_kbase_jm.c:410-415) is gated on JSn_STATUS==0, and we read 0x08.
answers.3_address_space: THE PER-AS PROGRAMMING IS EQUIVALENT. Vendor kbase_mmu_update (mali_kbase_mem.c:632-670): TRANSTAB_LO = (pgd & 0xFFFFF000) | ASn_TRANSTAB_READ_INNER(1<<2) | ADRMODE_TABLE(3); HI=0; MEMATTR_LO = kctx->mem_attrs low word; MEMATTR_HI=0; then ASn_COMMAND=UPDATE. Our p7580_mmu_program_as (panfrost7580_mmu.c:337-356): TRANSTAB = pgd|P7580_TRANSTAB_FLAGS (=3|1<<2, panfrost7580_mmu.h:81), MEMATTR_LO/HI from the caller (main.c:777/390, job.c:1563 pass P7580_MEMATTR_KBASE_LO=0x884D4F48 / HI=0x00008D88, mmu.h:96-97), then TRANSCFG_LO(0x30)=0, wmb, UPDATE. Deltas: (i) our memattr table also fills indices 3..5 (0x88/0x88/0x8D) while the vendor leaves them 0 - unused, because PTEs use index 0 (P7580_MEMATTR_IDX_DEFAULT, submit.c:1272) and index 0 is 0x48 in BOTH tables (vendor mem_attrs built at mali_kbase_mmu.c:868-873); (ii) we write AS_TRANSCFG at 0x30 - a no-op in LPAE (AArch64-only register), it does not alias MEMATTR(0x08) or STATUS(0x28); (iii) our ATEs set AF (1<<10) while the vendor's kbase_mmu_get_mmu_flags never sets ENTRY_ACCESS_BIT (mali_kbase_mmu.c:470-500, the bit is defined but unused, mali_kbase_defs.h:131) - AF=1 is the safe direction and cannot produce a translation fault (AF=0 could produce an ACCESS_FLAG 0xD8 fault). PTE body/flags are otherwise byte-identical (ate = phys|memattr<<2|RD|WR|NX|ATE, vendor mali_kbase_mmu.c:307-330, defs.h:126-136, 4-level walk with MIDGARD_MMU_VA_BITS 48 -> TOPLEVEL 0, defs.h:133-139; ours panfrost7580_mmu.c:249-306 with P7580_MMU_LEVELS 4). CONSEQUENCE: MEMATTR/shareability/TRANSTAB cannot be what turns a BO access into a translation fault; the fault is a genuinely absent leaf entry.
answers.4_tiler_heap: THIS VENDOR KBASE HAS NO TILER-HEAP CODE AT ALL (grep 'tiler_heap'/'TILER_HEAP' over the whole midgard/ tree: no hits), i.e. on this DDK the heap is 100% userspace-owned - which matches Mesa, which allocates it once at screen creation (src/gallium/drivers/panfrost/pan_device.c:103-105, 128 MiB, PAN_BO_INVISIBLE|PAN_BO_GROWABLE, 'Tiler heap') and passes start/size straight into the SFBD tiler section (pan_cmdstream.c:4774-4775, packed at pan_desc.c:1058-1059, heap_start=heap.start, heap_end=start+size). Mesa never writes into it, and it is submitted in bo_handles (mesa/diag/0001 patch:201 'bo_handles[...] = dev->tiler_heap->gem_handle'). So the 128 MB BO at IOVA 0x2000000 is exactly what kbase would hand the tiler, and there is no kernel-side heap/descriptor initialisation that we omit. What kbase DOES have and we omit is the fault side of the same machinery: KBASE_REG_GROWABLE on all tmem (mali_kbase_mem.c:967-968 'all memory is now growable') plus the page-fault grow path (mali_kbase_mmu.c:120-265): fault -> find growable region (:157) -> kbase_alloc_phy_pages_helper (:196) -> kbase_mmu_insert_pages (:215) -> LOCK/FLUSH_PT/UNLOCK (:205-250) -> mmu_mask_reenable; and the non-growable branch kills the job (kbase_mmu_report_fault_and_kill, :1338-1416). Our heap is pre-faulted (submit.c:1260-1275 maps every one of the BO's npages), so no grow is needed inside [0x2000000,0xa000000) - and indeed the fault is outside that range.
answers.5_descriptor_patching: THE VENDOR NEVER TOUCHES THE DESCRIPTOR. kbase_job_hw_submit only writes HEAD/AFFINITY/CONFIG/COMMAND (mali_kbase_jm.c:72-146); there is no read or write of the JD, the SFBD or the tiler section anywhere in kbase_jm.c (the descriptor is 100% userspace-built). Our submit path patches ONLY the 8 header words, and only when the node is shadowed: need_shadow = nodes>1 || dep1 || dep2 || any of w0..w3 nonzero (panfrost7580_submit.c:1949-1966), then p7580_chain_hdr_isolate() rewrites next/deps/index and w0..w3 are zeroed (:1991-2011). The fragment node is a single-node, zero-dep descriptor whose live words are sw=00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 00010013 (w0..w3 = 0), so need_shadow=0 and the ORIGINAL Mesa descriptor is dispatched verbatim ('A one-node chain with no dependency indices is already a standalone dispatch (Mesa's fragment submit): keep the original descriptor', :1946-1948). No kernel write to the JD/SFBD applies to the hanging job. (Aside: chain_mode==1 would OR JOB_CHAIN_FLAG from desc[4]&1, which is the job_descriptor_size bit - wrong source; verify chain_mode=0.)
answers.6_0b2aa000: Not expressible as a small delta from the heap: heap_end is 0x0a000000 (heap = 0x2000000 + 0x8000000, first-fit from P7580_IOVA_START=32MiB, panfrost7580_gem.h:70-71), so 0x0b2aa000 - 0x0a000000 = 0x12aa000 = 4778 pages = 18.66 MiB - no structural meaning. The one map-relative identity that is exact: 0x0b2aa000 = framebuffer BO base 0x0aeee000 + 0x3bc000, i.e. 956 pages past the RT base and 48 pages (0x30000) past the end of that 0x38c000 BO (end 0x0b27a000). Two consequences worth using: (a) it is in the same 2 MiB L3-table region as the FB BO's tail [0xb200000,0xb400000) - which is why the code is 0xC3 (translation fault at the LEAF level, kbase decode 0xC0-0xC7, mali_kbase_mmu.c:1305-1318) and not 0xC0/0xC1/0xC2: the walk finds valid L0/L1/L2 tables because the FB BO occupies the start of that region, and dies on the one leaf that is unmapped; (b) access type = READ ((0x090002c3>>8)&3 = 2, same decode kbase prints at mali_kbase_mmu.c:1362-1366) and bit 10 clear = 'SLAVE FAULT'. A READ that runs off the END of the render target is what a clean-pixel/tile-buffer LOAD produces (the SFBD has Clean Pixel Write Enable set; a plain render-target write would report access type WRITE 0x3). Weighted hypothesis: the SFBD tells the GPU an RT pitch/height that exceeds the 0x38c000 BO - e.g. a 1024-px-rounded pitch (4096 B/row) over 1280 rows = 5,238,784 B vs the 3,727,360-byte BO; the first out-of-range tile row then faults at a fixed, deterministic offset. Decisive check: SFBD +0x60 (Color Writeback Base) and +0x64 (Row Stride) vs the BO size, plus the fault-time page dump of the polygon list body. The 0x0900 in FAULTSTATUS[31:16] (kbase's 'source id' print) is not a plausible core id on a 2-core T720; treat as unexplained/informational.

ranked_causes.cause: UNRESOLVED MMU PAGE FAULT STALLS THE FRAGMENT JOB'S EXECUTOR (mechanism, effectively proven by the register set).
ranked_causes.evidence: PORT: panfrost7580_main.c:76-119 p7580_drv_mmu_irq() reads MMU_INT_STAT, logs 'panfrost7580: MMU fault AS%u: %s/%s stat %08x addr %08x%08x' (:110) and writes MMU_INT_CLEAR (:117) - nothing else; there is no grow, no AS-unmapped switch, no slot stop, no job kill anywhere in the driver (grep TRANSTAB/UNMAPPED/grow: only p7580_mmu_program_as and submit-time invalidate). MMU_INT_MASK=0xFFFFFFFF at init/rearm (panfrost7580_job.c:361-362), so faults are delivered and our handler consumes the latch - which is why TIMEOUT-DIAG reads MMU_RAWSTAT=0 while AS0 FAULTSTATUS stays latched. VENDOR: mali_kbase_mmu.c:1097-1200 masks the AS, latches fault_addr/fault_status, clears the bit and queues a worker which either grows (mali_kbase_mmu.c:157-256) or kills+resets (kbase_mmu_report_fault_and_kill :1338-1416), always ending in mmu_mask_reenable; kbase's CFS policy additionally soft-stops, hard-stops and then resets the GPU (mali_kbase_js_policy_cfs.c:720-773) so a slot is never left ACTIVE. Corroboration that the wedged block is the fragment job's executor: pf7580_cores_off_locked() logs 'tiler did not idle on power-off, aborting suspend' (panfrost7580_power.c:276-283) - the tiler never acknowledges PWRON=0, i.e. it is still mid-transaction, and JS_STATUS 0x08 is BASE_JD_EVENT_ACTIVE ('jobs only returned on complete/fail/cancel', mali_base_kernel.h:751).
ranked_causes.experiment: (a) ZERO COST: grep dmesg for 'MMU fault AS0' - one line per TIMEOUT proves the mechanism. (b) MINIMAL PATCH (test-only, ~8 lines in panfrost7580_main.c): in p7580_drv_mmu_irq(), for the faulting AS take the driver's job device and (i) write HARD_STOP to the faulting slot's CURRENT command register (regs + 0x1800 + slot*0x80 + 0x20, value 3), (ii) call the existing recover path (p7580_job_recover) or kick the job timeout work. Expected: the job retires immediately with ERR/TERMINATED instead of a 750 ms TIMEOUT, the drain loop exits, recover-done shows latched=0x03/0x04 and drain_rc=0, and the next cores_off no longer prints 'tiler did not idle'.
ranked_causes.log_delta_proves: PROVES: an 'MMU fault AS0: TRANSLATION_FAULT/READ ... addr 0b2aa000' line immediately preceding every TIMEOUT, plus disappearance of the silent 0x08 timeouts once the fault is acted on. DISPROVES: no MMU fault line at all in dmesg (then the FAULTSTATUS/FAULTADDRESS are stale leftovers and the stall has another cause, e.g. R4/R5).

ranked_causes.cause: THE BOGUS POINTER: the fragment job READS 48 pages past the end of the 0x38c000 render-target BO (0x0aeee000 + 0x3bc000 = 0x0b2aa000), i.e. an RT pitch/height that exceeds the BO.
ranked_causes.evidence: Arithmetic against the ERR-MAP in the ticket: 0x0b2aa000 = 0x0aeee000 + 0x3bc000 = 956 pages; FB BO = 0xaeee000/0x38c000, end 0xb27a000, so the fault is exactly 0x30000 past it and inside the same 2 MiB table region (which is why the fault is level-3, 0xC3). Access type is READ (0x2), which a render-target WRITE cannot produce but a clean-pixel/tile-buffer LOAD can; the SFBD's Clean Pixel Write Enable was measured set (gpu31-fbdtarget.md §2, Parameters +0x20). Port never writes the SFBD (submit.c:1946-2014 covers header words only). Vendor equivalent: nothing - kbase would take this exact fault to kbase_mmu_report_fault_and_kill (mali_kbase_mmu.c:157-160: region not found/growable mismatch -> kill).
ranked_causes.experiment: Arm the existing fault dumper (desc_dump + p7580_job_first_fault, panfrost7580_job.c:279-341) so the 'fbd' page is printed, then read SFBD +0x60 (Color Writeback Base), +0x64 (Row Stride), +0x28/+0x2C (bound min/max), +0xC0..+0xE0 (tiler section: polygon_list_size/hierarchy/pl/pl_body/heap_start/heap_end). Compare 'RT base + stride*rows' with the owning BO's size from ERR-MAP. Second half: dump the polygon list header/body and check whether any entry points at 0xb2aa000 or is out of its own BO.
ranked_causes.log_delta_proves: PROVES: (RT base == 0xaeee000) and (stride*height > 0x38c000), or a tiler-section field whose value lands on 0xb2aa000/0xb200000. DISPROVES: SFBD stride/bounds that fit the BO exactly and all tiler-section pointers in-range (then the pointer is a runtime value, e.g. a stale polygon-list entry -> see R3).

ranked_causes.cause: RECOVERY STOPS THE WRONG REGISTER VIEW: HARD_STOP is written to JS_COMMAND_NEXT (0x60) so the CURRENT job is never stopped; the stall survives every recovery (hence 'tiler did not idle' after each one).
ranked_causes.evidence: PORT: panfrost7580_job.c:1486-1492 p7580_js_write(jd, fault_slot, P7580_JS_COMMAND_NEXT, P7580_JS_CMD_HARD_STOP) and the drain loop at :1501 polls COMMAND_NEXT. VENDOR: kbase writes the stop to the CURRENT command register, kbase_reg_write(JOB_SLOT_REG(js, JSn_COMMAND), action, kctx) (mali_kbase_jm.c:553) - and only after checking COMMAND_NEXT: if COMMAND_NEXT==0 the job is current -> stop via JSn_COMMAND; else evict the queued next job with NOP first (mali_kbase_jm.c:694-706, 761-772). Register map: JSn_COMMAND 0x20 (current) vs JSn_COMMAND_NEXT 0x60 (next), mali_midg_regmap.h:228,238; our own header has both (panfrost7580_jm_hw.h:50,59).
ranked_causes.experiment: One-line swap at panfrost7580_job.c:1486: write P7580_JS_CMD_HARD_STOP to P7580_JS_COMMAND (offset 0x20) instead of P7580_JS_COMMAND_NEXT, and make the drain loop poll JSn_STATUS (0x24) != 0x08 instead of COMMAND_NEXT.
ranked_causes.log_delta_proves: PROVES: after recovery, JSn_STATUS moves 0x08 -> 0x03/0x04 (STOPPED/TERMINATED) and recover-done prints latched=0x03/0x04 with drain_rc=0, and the subsequent cores_off stops printing 'tiler did not idle'. DISPROVES: JS_STATUS still 0x08 after a HARD_STOP on 0x20 (the block is truly wedged and only a reset/power-cycle clears it - R1 remains, R3 is only a recovery defect).

ranked_causes.cause: GPU-LEVEL FAULTS ARE MASKED: the 'unmask like kbase' write goes to 0x1058 instead of GPU_IRQ_MASK 0x028, so GPU_FAULT (bit 0) is never delivered; the power slice leaves 0x028=0 in steady state. Any core-level error report at the moment of the stall is invisible.
ranked_causes.evidence: PORT: panfrost7580_jm_hw.h:95-96 defines P7580_GPU_IRQ_MASK as 0x1058 and ALL as 0x10581, written at panfrost7580_job.c:363 (readback printed at :365-368). panfrost7580_power.c:195/211 program the REAL 0x028 with RESET_COMPLETED only and then 0. VENDOR: GPU_IRQ_MASK is GPU_CONTROL_REG(0x028) (mali_midg_regmap.h:39) and kbase unmasks it with GPU_IRQ_REG_ALL (mali_kbase_pm_driver.c:597, mask value mali_midg_regmap.h:54-55), then kbase_gpu_interrupt reports GPU_FAULT and clears via GPU_IRQ_CLEAR (mali_kbase_device.c:371-400). Observed: GPU_INT_RAWSTAT=0x00000600 = POWER_CHANGED_SINGLE|POWER_CHANGED_ALL (mali_midg_regmap.h:49-52) still latched at timeout - proof the GPU IRQ handler is not draining it (panfrost7580_main.c:131-147 clears RAWSTAT only when the line fires).
ranked_causes.experiment: Write 0xFFFFFFFF to offset 0x0028 in p7580_job_irq_program() (both call sites) instead of 0x1058, and print the 0x028 readback. Then check the existing readback line 'gpu_irq_mask=0x10581(rd ...)' from the current build.
ranked_causes.log_delta_proves: PROVES: with 0x028 unmasked, GPU_INT_RAWSTAT=0x600 stops accumulating, and a GPU fault/exception line appears at hang time (revealing the core that faulted). DISPROVES: if the current dmesg already shows rd 0x00000000 right after the 0x10581 write and no GPU fault bit ever latches even when unmasked, R4 is diagnostic-only.

ranked_causes.cause: STALE/UNINITIALISED GPU-VISIBLE POINTER (polygon-list body or a recycled pool page) fed to the fragment job - the polygon list is not guaranteed zeroed before the tiler writes it, and our chain split dispatches each node with its own START.
ranked_causes.evidence: Mesa writes the T720 magic 0xa0000000 into polygon_list_body only when there are NO draws (pan_cmdstream.c:4760-4771); with draws the body is whatever the BO contained (BO cache reuse). Our split path re-dispatches each node from a shadow only when needed and isolates next/deps/index (panfrost7580_submit.c:1968-2014), and it never validates pointers inside the GPU-written list. gpu31-jddecode/gpu31-firstfault document exactly this class of stale-pool-content fault in this driver.
ranked_causes.experiment: Add a fault-time census of the polygon-list BO (pl, pl_body from SFBD +0xC8/+0xD0): count entries that fall outside the heap BO, and print the first 8 entries. Also force Mesa to zero the list (or add a kernel-side memset of the polygon-list BO at map time) and see whether the fault address changes.
ranked_causes.log_delta_proves: PROVES: an entry in the polygon list whose value equals 0xb2aa000 (or whose in-heap-ness is false) at fault time. DISPROVES: a completely in-range polygon list (then the pointer is not data-driven - back to R2).

ranked_causes.cause: DESCRIPTOR/TILER-CONTEXT TEARING between SUBMIT and the GPU's fetch (the gpu31-jddecode family).
ranked_causes.evidence: Real for earlier faults (0x52/0x58 at head=tail=jc), fixed by the bo_count stamp + excl-fence publish (submit.c:2130-2165 publishes under serial_lock). But it cannot be the current signature: JS_STATUS is ACTIVE(0x08) with no exception code and no ERROR bit, whereas a torn descriptor yields a JS_STATUS fault code and an ERR interrupt (measured 0x52/0x58 in gpu31-fbdtarget.md §5.5).
ranked_causes.experiment: None needed beyond R1's dmesg check; if desired, re-run with the existing 'desc-stale ... (shadowed+sanitised)' print enabled and confirm it is absent for the fragment node.
ranked_causes.log_delta_proves: DISPROVES itself: presence of a JS_STATUS >= 0x40 ERR at dispatch would re-open this; the observed 0x08 does not.

ranked_causes.cause: IRQ/MASK LOSS OR A MISSING-INTERRUPT HARDWARE WORKAROUND (BASE_HW_ISSUE_10883).
ranked_causes.evidence: t72x carries 10883 (mali_base_hwconfig.h:525-539) and kbase works around a *missing interrupt* only when the slot still reads ACTIVE **and** JSn_STATUS==0 (mali_kbase_jm.c:410-415). We read 0x08. A masked DONE (the hang_inject knob added for exactly this test, panfrost7580_job.c:687-697) would leave RAWSTAT latched, not 0.
ranked_causes.experiment: Read the hang_arm knob (debugfs) to confirm it is 0; optionally set it to 1 and compare the signature with the observed one.
ranked_causes.log_delta_proves: PROVES (as a control): hang_inject reproduces 'stat=0 rawstat=0 ACTIVE 0x08 TIMEOUT' only when the mask is deliberately broken - which is why the observed run must be checked for hang_arm!=0 before dismissing it.

ruled_out_by_registers: rawstat=0 / stat=0: no DONE and no ERR was ever posted by the JM for slot 0, and no bit is latched-and-masked. A lost, masked or mis-cleared DONE would leave JOB_INT_RAWSTAT set (it is a latch: mali_midg_regmap.h:194-196). Combined with JS_STATUS=0x08=BASE_JD_EVENT_ACTIVE (mali_base_kernel.h:751) this eliminates every 'completion side' theory (R7) and any IRQ handler bug.

head==tail==jc (0x18b97c80) with COMMAND_NEXT drained: the START was consumed, the descriptor was fetched and the chain was walked to the single job - so no swallowed START, no JS_CONFIG/affinity/descriptor-size problem, no chain-flag problem (R6 partially), and the classic 'job never started' failure mode is out.

js ACTIVE(0x08) with no exception code: the JM is not reporting CONFIG/AFFINITY/READ/WRITE/INSTR faults; therefore submit-order, cfg value (0x83700|as_nr), TS priorities and the descriptor header are not the immediate blocker - the job is *alive* and blocked, which is only consistent with a stalled memory transaction (R1) - not with a bad job encoding.

Fault address constant and outside every BO, plus the code being 0xC3 (leaf-level translation fault) and access READ (0x2): not a permission fault (0xC8), not a bus fault (0xD0-0xD7), not an access-flag fault (0xD8) - so no TRANSTAB/MEMATTR/shareability/AF misconfiguration is involved (R3 in the answers: per-AS programming and PTE flags are equivalent to kbase; our AF=1 is stricter).

MMU_RAWSTAT=0 at timeout while AS0 FAULTSTATUS/FAULTADDRESS stay latched: the fault interrupt is delivered, handled and cleared by our handler (mask is 0xFFFFFFFF), i.e. the driver *knows* about the fault and does nothing - confirming R1 rather than a missing-interrupt scenario.

GPU_INT_RAWSTAT=0x600 (POWER_CHANGED_SINGLE|ALL) permanently latched: no GPU-level fault is pending (bit 0 clear), so the stall is not a GPU_FAULT event that we failed to service; it also independently shows the GPU IRQ line is mis-masked (R4) but that is a visibility bug, not the hang.
experiment_order: 1. grep dmesg before the first TIMEOUT for 'panfrost7580: MMU fault' (zero cost, settles R1).
2. check the existing readback 'gpu_irq_mask=0x10581(rd 0x........)' and the debugfs hang_arm value (zero cost, settles R4 and the R7 control).
3. arm desc_dump/ev_arm, reproduce once, read the 'fbd' page dump: SFBD +0x60/+0x64/+0x28/+0x2C and the tiler section +0xC0..+0xE0 (settles R2; also feeds R5).
4. test-only patch: HARD_STOP via JSn_COMMAND (0x20) in the MMU IRQ handler + recovery; expect ERR/TERMINATED instead of the silent 0x08 timeout (R1/R3).

5. if the stop still does not take, the block is wedged at fabric level: the only kbase-equivalent remedy left is the full reset/power-cycle path that recovery already owns - which is why 'tiler did not idle' aborts suspend afterwards.

arguments.content:
AF is not the regression — refuted by both trees, and the fix would be the opposite of what you propose.

1) Our ATE always carries AF, from the ONLY leaf writer: panfrost7580_mmu.c:290-292 `leaf = (paddr & ADDR_MASK) | P7580_PTE_TYPE_ATE | (memattr_idx<<2) | P7580_PTE_AF_BIT`, and grep shows P7580_PTE_TYPE_ATE/P7580_PTE_AF_BIT appear nowhere else (single writer; teardown writes only ENTRY_IS_INVAL=2).
2) The vendor kbase NEVER sets it: kbase_mmu_get_mmu_flags (mali_kbase_mmu.c:470-500) ORs only memattr<<2, WR(1<<6), RD(1<<7), NX(1<<54), share(9:8); ENTRY_ACCESS_BIT (mali_kbase_defs.h:131) is defined and used NOWHERE (only in the ENTRY_FLAGS_MASK define at :134). So this exact T720 runs the stock driver with AF=0 everywhere. If AF=1 were required, kbase would fault and it doesn't; if AF=1 were harmful, we'd be looking at it — so a "missing AF" story can't explain anything. Matching kbase byte-for-byte means CLEARING bit 10, not adding it.

So the 0xD8 needs a different reading. What it does tell us:
- 0xD8 = ACCESS_FLAG per kbase's own table (mali_kbase_mmu.c:1324-1326 = BASE_JD_EVENT_ACCESS_FLAG 0xD8). It is a *different class* from the KWin stall we are chasing (0xC3 translation fault, leaf absent) — don't merge the two.
- Your 4 faults are non-fatal (job completes, rawstat=0x1/0x2 latched then demuxed), which fits *dropped/speculative* transactions, not a wedged slot. Page-aligned triples inside live BOs + one mid-page (0x…55c0) means the leaves are found, so this is not "BO not mapped"; it is either a stale uTLB/first-touch visibility artifact or a genuinely AF=0 entry the hardware read.

Two experiments settle it in one boot:
A) At fault time, software-walk the driver's page tables from drv->mmu.root_dma for the faulting VA and print the level-3 ATE (u64 hex). If RAM says type=1|AF=1|memattr=0 and the hardware still faults, the entry is right → stale-TLB/visibility. If RAM says 0x2/0x0, our write never landed or was overwritten → find the writer (that would be a real bug, and would also explain the checksum flip).
B) Build one variant with bit 10 cleared (P7580_PTE_AF_BIT removed) to match kbase byte-exactly. Same faults → AF fully exonerated; faults vanish → this part mis-uses bit 10 and that is the finding. Either outcome is one flash.
C) Free datum: grep the #37 dmesg (the build with stable checksums) for "MMU fault". If the same 4x ACCESS_FLAG/draw were already there, they are noise and your checksum flip is a coherency/lifetime bug, not the faults.

On the alternating checksum + zeros at +300 ms: that pattern is "read before the GPU's writes are visible / BO recycled", not "attribute pages dropped". 0x8b…/0x83… alternating between runs = a fence/provenance problem: verify the readback BO is inside the fragment job's bo_handles (only those get the DONE-path invalidate via p7580_gem_job_bos_pre_signal_sync, panfrost7580_job.c:936-940), and that glFinish waits on that job's out_sync rather than a later submit's (per-file serial_prev publishing is under df->serial_lock, submit.c:2126-2165). "All zeros later" additionally smells of the BO being freed and re-zeroed while your process still maps it — check bo_age/iova reuse for that range.

Also relevant to your fault attribution: in this port an IOVA is assigned at CREATE_BO (panfrost7580_gem.c:902 p7580_iova_alloc) but page-table leaves are written ONLY by p7580_drv_map_bo from the SUBMIT handle list (panfrost7580_submit.c:1208-1290, called at :1841-1862). A created-but-never-submitted BO therefore has a valid IOVA and no leaves, unlike kbase which maps at mmap/alloc time (kbase_gpu_mmap). So "inside a BO the process created" does not imply "mapped". Please eyeball whether the 4 faulting pages belong to a BO that appeared in ANY submit's bo_handles.

I have file:line answers for all six comparison questions (submit seq, DONE/IRQ, AS+PTE, tiler heap, descriptor patching, the 0xb2aa000 identity); the KWin stall's mechanism is an unresolved translation fault that our MMU IRQ handler only logs+clears (panfrost7580_main.c:76-119) while kbase grows or kills+resets (mali_kbase_mmu.c:157-256, 1338-1416) — plus recovery stopping via COMMAND_NEXT instead of JSn_COMMAND (job.c:1486 vs mali_kbase_jm.c:553, 694-706). Ask if you want any of that detail.

Replied to `Mesa203Build`; my earlier terminal report to Main stands.

**What I sent (for the record):**

1. **"AF is not carried" is refuted from both trees.** Our only leaf writer sets it (`panfrost7580_mmu.c:290-292`, and `P7580_PTE_TYPE_ATE`/`P7580_PTE_AF_BIT` appear nowhere else), while the stock vendor kbase *never* sets it — `kbase_mmu_get_mmu_flags` (`mali_kbase_mmu.c:470-500`) ORs only memattr<<2, RD/WR, NX and share bits, and `ENTRY_ACCESS_BIT` (`mali_kbase_defs.h:131`) is dead code. A port that sets AF cannot be faulting for lack of AF, and matching kbase would mean *clearing* bit 10, not adding it.

2. **What the 0xD8 actually is:** `ACCESS_FLAG` per kbase's own table (`mali_kbase_mmu.c:1324-1326`), a different fault class from the fragment-job stall (0xC3 translation fault at 0x0b2aa000). Their faults are non-fatal (job completes; JOB_INT rawstat 0x1/0x2 latched then demuxed), so the two must not be merged.

3. **Three cheap discriminators:** software-walk the page tables at fault time and print the level-3 ATE (type/AF/memattr decides stale-TLB vs. missing entry); one flash with bit 10 cleared to match kbase byte-exactly; and grep the #37 dmesg (the stable-checksum build) for the same 4 faults/draw.

4. **Redirect for the alternating checksum:** that signature is a fence/provenance problem (read before visibility, or BO recycled to zeros), so check the readback BO is in the fragment job's `bo_handles` (only those get the DONE-path invalidate) and that `glFinish` waits on that job's out_sync. I also flagged a port-specific hole worth ruling out for their faulting pages: IOVAs are assigned at `CREATE_BO` (`gem.c:902`) but leaves are written only for BOs in a SUBMIT handle list (`submit.c:1208-1290`, `:1841-1862`), so "inside a BO the process created" does not imply "mapped" — unlike kbase, which maps at mmap/alloc time.

content.thinking:
New data is extremely informative. Let me analyze carefully.

Key facts:
1. FAULTSTATUS = 0x800002d8, FAULTADDRESS = 0x299a55c0 = the **jc address itself** (the fragment job descriptor!). Access type READ (0x2 in bits 9:8: 0x2d8 → (0x2d8>>8)&3 = 2 → READ). Code 0xD8 = ACCESS_FLAG.
2. The driver's own PTEWALK says: leaf = 0x66f244c1 = ATE(1) | RD(0x40) | WR(0x80) | AF(0x400) | memattr 0. leaf_phys == bo_phys. So the leaf in the level-3 table is valid WITH AF.

Wait: 0x66f244c1. Let's decode: 0x...4c1: low bits 0x4c1 = 0b0100_1100_0001: bit0=1 (ATE), bits 6(0x40),7(0x80) = RD|WR, bit10 (0x400) = AF, memattr bits 4:2 = 0. Yes: 0x4c1 = 1 + 0x40 + 0x80 + 0x400. Good.

So the leaf HAS AF, and yet the hardware reports ACCESS_FLAG fault at that very address (the JC). Wow.

What does that mean? The hardware has *not* seen the entry we wrote → a **stale uTLB / page-table coherency** problem. The hardware read an OLD version of that entry (from a previous BO at that IOVA, or a zero/invalid entry) and cached it, and our TLB maintenance didn't take effect for that entry.

But hold on: the access is a READ at the JC = the **job descriptor fetch by the JM**. The JM fetches the job descriptor through the MMU. And the fault is ACCESS_FLAG. Hmm, the JM's descriptor fetch faulting with ACCESS_FLAG while the leaf is valid-with-AF → strongly suggests the MMU's uTLB holds a stale entry for that page: an entry that existed *before* we wrote the leaf — e.g. when the page table entry was in the INVALID state (0x2). But an invalid entry (type 2 = "translation fault" marker) should give translation fault 0xC0-0xC7, not 0xD8...

Unless: an entry of 0x0 (type 0 = "invalid/fault") gives a *different* fault class (0xD8 ACCESS_FLAG) than type 2! Interesting hypothesis: Midgard MMU ATE types: 1 = ATE (valid page), 2 = invalid (unmapped), 3 = PTE (table). A 0x0 entry might be interpreted as "fault" → ACCESS_FLAG? Hmm.

Hmm wait, but there's something even more interesting: the *pattern*. 3 faults per run, size-independent. 3 faults, at: 0x29dcb000/0x29dcb100/0x29dcb200 (3 consecutive pages of BO 12 = the 4MB FBO) and 0x299a55c0 (jc page). That's 4 in the earlier report, 3 now. Size-independent → constant set of pages, likely one per BO/one per *newly mapped page*.

Key insight candidate: These are the pages that were mapped **most recently** — 3 of them — i.e. the first accesses after a fresh map on a page whose uTLB entry is stale.

Now, why does this hang the fragment job at the *jc address*? Because the JM's descriptor fetch at jc faults → the JM stops fetching → the job never starts... but JS_STATUS says ACTIVE(0x08) and HEAD==TAIL==jc, meaning the JM *did* latch the head. Hmm: HEAD==TAIL==jc means the JM loaded the head pointer and... the descriptor fetch faulted. So the job entered "ACTIVE" (head latched) but is blocked on the descriptor fetch. That's precisely "enters execution (HEAD==TAIL) but never posts DONE/ERR" — and it matches my R1 mechanism (unresolved fault → stall), but now the *trigger* is not a bogus pointer from Mesa; it's a stale-invalid uTLB entry for the job descriptor's own page.

This upgrades the diagnosis: it's a **page-table/TLB coherency bug in the port**, not a Mesa pointer bug. The fault address being exactly the jc explains "constant across jobs" (each job's own jc page).

Now: the PTEWALK MATCH (leaf_phys == bo_phys) proves the tables in DRAM (as read by the CPU) are correct. So the GPU's view differs → either:
(a) the page-table page was written by the CPU but not made visible to the GPU (cache: our `dma_sync_single_for_device` on the PT page may be a no-op if the page was never dma_mapped for the device, or `p7580_kmap_dma`/kmap writes go through a cache that isn't cleaned);
(b) the MMU's uTLB still holds an older translation and our LOCK/FLUSH/UNLOCK sequence doesn't flush the right region or is issued in the wrong order;
(c) the mapping happens *after* the job was already dispatched (a race: map then START without a TLB flush in between? we do invalidate before/after).

Crucially: the port's `p7580_mmu_invalidate()` is called from the submit path *before* the leaf writes (with sync=1 → FLUSH_MEM) and after (sync=0 → FLUSH_PT). Let's look at the kbase function this was modeled on: `kbase_mmu_hw_do_operation` — kbase acquires the AS transaction lock, does LOCK → op → wait → UNLOCK. And importantly, kbase does the TLB invalidation *after* inserting the pages AND the operation types: FLUSH_PT flushes only the page table cache; FLUSH_MEM = flush all L2s + region.

Hmm, and note the port's invalidate implementation order: 
```
LOCK; FLUSH; wait_ready; UNLOCK
```
And `p7580_as_wait_ready` polls AS_STATUS & ACTIVE. Then UNLOCK. But note: it doesn't *wait* after UNLOCK, and more importantly there's a subtlety in kbase: for BASE_HW_ISSUE_9630, kbase issues **two UNLOCK commands** ("As the region is now unlocked we need to issue 2 UNLOCK commands in order to flush the MMU/uTLB, see PRLAM-8812", mali_kbase_mmu.c:245-251). Our port issues ONE unlock (mmu.c:407), with a comment claiming it flushes. t72x's issue list (base_hwconfig.h:525-539) does NOT include 9630 — let me check: the t72x list I read: 6402, 8803, 8975, 9435, 10472, 10649, 10684, 10797, 10821, 10883, 10931, 10946, 10959. No 9630. So double-unlock isn't required on t72x per kbase. Hmm. But wait — the port's comment at mmu.c:405-407 says "UNLOCK flushes the MMU/uTLB so updated entries are re-read (kbase BASE_HW_ISSUE_9630 note)". If 9630 isn't in the t72x issue list, kbase wouldn't do it for t72x. But our port does it unconditionally, which is harmless.

Hmm. Let me think about the *most likely* root cause given "leaf in DRAM is right, hardware faults ACCESS_FLAG on the JC page, 3 faults/run, size-independent, intermittent TIMEOUT".

ACCESS_FLAG at an address whose ATE has AF=1... For ARM, an AF fault means the descriptor had AF=0. Which descriptor? If the walk hits the L2 *table* descriptor... we write table entries as `(dma & ~0xFFF) | 3` = type PTE(3), bit10 = 0! Hmm!! For a table descriptor, bit 10 in ARM LPAE is SBZ/reserved. One root cause covers both of your symptoms: whichever first access lands on a stale entry gets its transaction dropped — data read dropped = garbage/alternating checksum (job still completes), descriptor fetch dropped = HEAD latched, JS_STATUS ACTIVE 0x08, no DONE/ERR (your hang). Nothing Mesa ever wrote was read in that job — recover-done js0=0 confirms the JM never got the descriptor.

The port has NO AS serialization at all. panfrost7580_mmu.h:109-114 declares a contract ("alloc/free/map/unmap: caller MUST hold the driver's MMU/table lock ... program_as/invalidate: caller MUST hold the MMU-HW lock"), but grep for mmu_lock/mmu_hw_lock/as_lock over the whole tree returns nothing — the field does not exist. In the submit path the only locks are drv->bo_lock (BO list) and df->serial_lock (fence publishing); p7580_drv_map_bo (panfrost7580_submit.c:1208-1290) and its two p7580_mmu_invalidate() calls run unlocked. kbase, by contrast, brackets every LOCK..FLUSH..UNLOCK in kbdev->as[n].transaction_mutex (mali_kbase_mmu.c:604-651) and every walk/insert in kctx->reg_lock. AS0 has exactly one LOCKADDR and one COMMAND: two interleaved publishers overwrite each other's LOCKADDR and the first one's FLUSH is applied to the wrong region (or finds nothing locked), so that range's new PTEs are never invalidated — 3 stale first-touches per run, size-independent, intermittent, fits perfectly. The second publisher in your single-threaded test is the recovery/resume path: p7580_mmu_program_as() runs from the job workqueue (panfrost7580_job.c:1563) and from resume (main.c:390) — i.e. exactly while a SUBMIT may be mid-map.

Tests, in order:
1. Add one struct mutex (as_lock) in p7580_drv; take it around the whole p7580_drv_map_bo body (both invalidates + the map loop) and around every p7580_mmu_program_as() + p7580_job_dev_rearm() call site (job.c:1563, main.c:390, main.c:777). Expect 3 faults/run -> 0 and stable checksums. This is the one I would bet on.
2. Independently: make the publish invalidate sync=1 (submit.c:1277) to match kbase's FLUSH_MEM.
3. If faults survive both, test IOVA-reuse: temporary monotonic bump allocator (no free/reuse) for one build. Faults vanish => stale uTLB on reused ranges; then the fix is a full-AS flush at unmap/alloc, kbase-style.
4. Diagnostic worth adding once: print ASn_STATUS and ASn_COMMAND right after p7580_as_wait_ready() in the publish path; a FLUSH issued with nothing locked (bit already clear, no work done) is visible there and would prove the interleaving directly.

Also: 0x299cb000 + 0x400000 = 0x29dcb000, so those three "FBO" fault pages are the first 3 pages of whatever BO starts *after* the 4 MB FBO, not inside it — re-check that attribution; if that BO belongs to a later submit it explains why the ERR-MAP of this submit doesn't cover it. Your 1.2 s glFinish is the recovery signalling the fence, so per-run latency alone tells you whether a fetch fault (not just a data fault) happened.

Sent. Summary of what their data changed and what I concluded:

**Their walk refutes the ATE/flag theories and pins the class of bug.** `leaf=0x66f244c1` (ATE|RD|WR|AF|memattr 0, `leaf_phys==bo_phys`, MATCH) while the GPU reports `ACCESS_FLAG` at that same VA means the hardware consumed a translation that does not match DRAM — i.e. the new PTE was never invalidated in the uTLB/GPU-L2. AF, memattr, TRANSTAB, and even the LOCKADDR width encoding are exonerated (I checked kbase's `lock_region` at `mali_kbase_mmu.c:1009-1040`: our encoder is identical, and t72x has neither issue 6367 nor 9630, so kbase uses the plain `FLUSH_MEM` branch there).

**The concrete defect: the port has no AS serialization at all.** `panfrost7580_mmu.h:109-114` states a locking contract ("caller MUST hold the driver's MMU/table lock", "MUST hold the MMU-HW lock"), but no such lock exists anywhere in the tree — the submit path only holds `bo_lock`/`serial_lock`, and `p7580_drv_map_bo` runs its two `p7580_mmu_invalidate()` calls unlocked. <irc>
Incoming IRC message from agent `Mesa203Build`:

Two data points that close your open questions, plus one negative result.

1) Attribution corrected, and the "3 pages" are NOT in any BO. Last-created BO end == first fault VA in every run:
- 64x64 run: BO 12 = 0x29644000/0x10000 -> end 0x29654000; faults 0x29654000, 0x29654100, 0x29654200.
- 720x1280 run: BO 12 = 0x299cb000/0x400000 (FBO) -> end 0x29dcb000; faults 0x29dcb000/100/200.

2) Fault class vs outcome, 8 consecutive 64x64 runs (same binary): descriptor fault at jc+0x5c0 in 7/8 runs, slot timeout in 1/8. Wall time 1.17-1.23 s when no recovery vs 2.55/3.41 s when recovery fired. Discriminator holds: data faults = stat 0x810002d8 (bit24 set), descriptor fetch = 0x800002d8 (bit24 clear). One outlier: the run that timed out (wall 3.41 s) showed only data faults in the ring, no descriptor line — either the line was lost or that recovery had a different trigger; ring wrap is possible, dmesg here is very chatty.

3) Negative result on my side, so don't chase it: I A/B'd stock 20.3.5 against the patched binary (patch 0007 touches exactly the attribute-descriptor array: it removes upstream's `memset(bufs + last, 0, ...)` n+1 prefetch suppression and zeroes/extends the arrays). Stock shows the SAME 3 page-past-end fault VAs (0x29654000/100/200) and the same jc-fetch class, with jc+0x580 instead of +0x5c0 (different descriptor layout). So the over-read is not caused by that patch; if anything stock recovered more often (3 timeouts in 4 runs vs 1 in 8), consistent with the patch helping slightly, sample too small to claim it.

Current shipped stack is the patched build again (install tree re-verified: panfrost_dri.so sha256 ef8c5cfb…6f46, 22 names one inode, GL_RENDERER/GL_VERSION PASS, eglSwapBuffers ok), so your test 1/2 (as_lock around p7580_drv_map_bo + program_as/rearm, and sync=1 FLUSH_MEM publish) lands on a known-good userspace baseline. I have nothing further to add on the kernel side — the as_lock interleaving story is the only mechanism that explains "DRAM leaf correct, hardware translation not".
If response expected, reply via `write` (`path: "agent://Mesa203Build"`, `content: "…"`), when available; otherwise what you `yield` or say last this turn is delivered to `Mesa203Build` when you stop.

So for their runs: "last BO end == fault VA" is then just "the top of the address space" — the reader is reading *above everything*. What's at the top? Nothing. So the reader's pointer ≈ top-of-allocator. Hmm, that smells like a **pointer built from an allocation's end rather than its start** (e.g. `base + size` used as a data pointer), where base is the last BO.

Let me look at their numbers once more: 64x64 run: BO 12 = 0x29644000/0x10000 → the fault is at 0x29654000 = BO12 end. 720 run: BO 12 = FBO 0x299cb000/0x400000 → fault 0x29dcb000 = FBO end.

arguments.content:
Read your numbers again: 0x29654000 / 0x29654100 / 0x29654200 are 0x100 = 256 bytes apart, so that is THREE LOADS INSIDE ONE PAGE at 256-byte stride, not three pages. Same for the 720 run (0x29dcb000/b100/b200). That changes the reading twice over, and it points somewhere we have not looked yet.

(a) They are at the first address past the highest BO, i.e. the IOVA that the NEXT allocation would start at. In the 64x64 run that BO is only 64 KiB, so the "last BO" is not the tiler heap; the constant is "just past whatever was allocated last", which is exactly what an access to a freshly allocated, as-yet-unmapped BO looks like. Remember the port only writes page-table leaves for BOs that appear in a SUBMIT's bo_handles (panfrost7580_submit.c:1208-1290, called from the handle loop at :1841-1862); an IOVA is assigned much earlier, at CREATE_BO (panfrost7580_gem.c:902). So "BO exists, IOVA valid, no leaf" is a normal state in this driver and kbase has no equivalent (kbase maps at mmap/alloc time, kbase_gpu_mmap). Three loads at 0x100 stride inside the first page of such a BO is exactly what a small descriptor-like structure read costs: first load faults, you clear, second and third fault the same way. This is the leading candidate for your data faults now — and it also explains the size independence (one fixed structure, not geometry).

(b) FAULTSTATUS/FAULTADDRESS are LATCHES (last fault, RO), and MMU_RAWSTAT was 0 at your timeout, so TIMEOUT-DIAG's address is only "the last fault the AS saw", not necessarily the one that stalled the job. Your own outlier run (3.41 s timeout, only data faults in the ring, no descriptor line) is direct evidence that the 0x08 stall does not require an MMU fault at all. Do not let TIMEOUT-DIAG's FAULTADDRESS drive the diagnosis; your bit-24 discriminator (0x810002d8 = data, 0x800002d8 = descriptor fetch) is the reliable tag, but tag from the IRQ-time log line ('MMU fault AS0: ... addr'), not from the timeout dump.

So the decisive experiment is cheap and needs no hardware theory: add a timestamped print in p7580_drv_map_bo of the IOVA range it maps (first page, page count, jiffies/ktime), and compare every 'MMU fault' line against it.
- fault at IOVA X BEFORE any map_bo covering X -> the GPU used a BO the driver had not mapped: submit/handle-list ordering hole (b above). Fix is mapping on create/mmap like kbase, or making Mesa list it.
- fault at IOVA X AFTER map_bo covering X -> genuinely stale translation: then as_lock + FLUSH_MEM publish. The missing AS lock (panfrost7580_mmu.h:109-114 states the contract, no such lock exists anywhere in the tree; kbase holds as[n].transaction_mutex around LOCK..FLUSH..UNLOCK, mali_kbase_mmu.c:604-651) remains a real bug either way — keep it, but it is no longer the only story.

Two cheap follow-ups while you are there:
1. In the MMU IRQ handler, also print the AS0 COMMAND/STATUS and the *current* JOB_INT_RAWSTAT, so you can tell "fault while a job is on the slot" from "fault during a map-time window".
2. Userspace-only A/B that costs no flash: give the tiler heap slack (allocate heap_end + 0x1000 or + one chunk, or 4x the size) and see whether the 3-load pattern moves to the new end or disappears. If it moves, the reader is addressing "heap_end + k*0x100" and the terminator/slack is the fix — which would also explain the KWin case, where the fault sits 0x12aa000 past the 128 MB heap end and FAULTADDRESS may in fact equal that run's heap_end (check heap_start/heap_end in the SFBD; if heap_end == 0xb2aa000 then the heap started at 0x32aa000 and the 0x2000000/0x8000000 BO in ERR-MAP is a different buffer).

Your stock-vs-0007 A/B killing the patch theory is useful and matches my reading: 0007 only touches the attribute-descriptor arrays, it cannot move an IOVA that is defined by the allocator's top.

Incoming IRC message from agent `Mesa203Build`:

Corrections and the decisive numbers, all measured on the shipped Mesa 20.3.5 stack unless stated.

1) My first pad/NODRAW run was invalid: it did not source the env, so it exercised the *system Mesa 26* (visible in its dmesg: tiler heap size=0x8000000, 128 MB). Both stacks nonetheless show the same fault families, which is itself a useful negative: these faults are not a Mesa-20.3.5 artifact.

2) Valid 20.3.5 numbers (64x64 FBO, env sourced, heap size=0x1000000 = the 16 MB from pan_props.c:231):
- draw, no pad: stat 0x810002d8 at 0x29654000, 0x29654100, 0x29654200 and stat 0x800002d8 at 0x2961e5c0 (inside the jc BO, +0x5c0). timeouts=0 that run.
- draw + 4 MB gbm pad BO on a second DRM fd: cluster moves to 0x39a5f000/f100/f200, descriptor fault 0x39a295c0. (The larger base is because the pad opened its own file, so IOVAs are per-file; the *shape* is unchanged.)
- NODRAW (glClear + glFinish only, draw skipped), 2/2 runs identical: exactly ONE fault, stat 0x800002d8 at 0x2961e280 (inside the jc BO, +0x280), no timeouts. So the 3 data faults at the top require the draw; a single descriptor-class fault happens even for a clear-only batch.
- Your 0x100 stride reading is confirmed: 3 loads inside one page at +0x0/+0x100/+0x200.

3) New fact that may matter more than the faults: in this kernel build, `p7580_iova: map` (submit.c:1307) never appears in dmesg — zero occurrences across all captures, while create_bo/sched/job lines are present in volume. If mapping really goes through p7580_drv_map_bo you'd expect one line per mapped BO per submit. 4) Mesa-side negative already reported: 0007 is not involved (stock shows the same cluster). content.thinking:
Critical finding! `p7580_drv_map_bo` **returns early (0) if the object is already in `drv->bo_list`**, and the bo_list entry is added once and removed only at GEM free (`p7580_gem_gpu_unmap`). So:

- The FIRST submit that references a BO maps it (one "p7580_iova: map" line, if the 64-line budget allows) and links it.
- Every subsequent submit returns early — **no map, no invalidate, no TLB flush for that BO**.
- And the bo_list is per-*driver*, so a BO stays linked (and mapped) for its whole life. That's actually fine and correct (map once).

So why zero "p7580_iova: map" lines? Because `p7580_iova_trace = 64` is a *global* budget consumed by... the trace starts at 64 at load. Those 64 lines are emitted over the first 64 fresh maps *since boot*. If any earlier process/mesa (e.g. the boot splash, or an earlier run) consumed them, later runs print nothing. Or... hmm, the peer says zero occurrences across all captures while create_bo lines are present "in volume". If create_bo lines are present (and those are NOT budgeted?), then BOs are being created but never *freshly mapped* — meaning they were already in bo_list... impossible for a brand-new BO.

Unless: `p7580_bo_npages(obj)` returns 0 → npages=0 → the map loop does nothing and the entry is still linked → "map ... npages=0" would print. Hmm, it would still print.

Wait, maybe pr_info is rate-limited/disabled? No, other pr_info lines appear.

Hmm! Critical: is the budget shared with other users? `p7580_iova_trace` is defined at submit.c:150 as a global initialized 64, decremented at 955 (unmap) and 1305 (map). So *unmaps consume the same budget*. If many BOs are freed early (Mesa frees transient BOs), the 64-line budget is consumed by unmap lines long before the interesting draw. So zero "map" lines can mean "budget exhausted by 'unmap' lines" — the peer should grep for "p7580_iova: unmap" too! If those are present, the budget explanation is settled.

That's a very clean, checkable answer: the budget is shared between map and unmap (submit.c:150, :955, :1305); grepping "p7580_iova: unmap" should show lines with numbers decreasing to 0.

But there's a much more important implication of the early-return: **a BO is mapped exactly once, at its first submit, and never re-mapped or re-invalidated afterwards.** Consequences:

1. If the same BO is used by *another GEM object* after free/recreate at the same IOVA — handled by unmap at free.
2. **The early return means no TLB invalidate is issued for the *other* BOs in later submits** — that's fine, they're already mapped.

NOW — the descriptor fault at jc+0x280/+0x5c0 *inside a mapped, submitted BO* (per PTEWALK MATCH) and the one fault even for a clear-only batch. Both are 0x800002d8 (bit24 clear). The clear-only case: the job chain (a WRITE_VALUE/clear job) is dispatched, and a fault is logged at jc+0x280 — inside the *descriptor's own page*! Wait: jc+0x280 is *inside the jc's page*? jc = 0x2961e280 would be the jc for the NODRAW run (the log line says the fault is at 0x2961e280 and the peer says "inside the jc BO, +0x280"). So the descriptor fault address == jc (the job's own address).

For NODRAW, the fault at 0x2961e280 = the *chain's jc* (the clear job's descriptor address), +0x280 into the pool BO.

So: in both cases, the fault address == **the job chain's own jc address** = the address the driver wrote into JS_HEAD_NEXT!

That is a huge, unifying observation: **the fault address is always the jc that the driver programmed into JSN_HEAD_NEXT.** And the fault class is the "descriptor" class (bit24 clear).

So the JM's *job fetch* itself faults, on the very page it is told to fetch. And PTEWALK says the leaf is correct... for the page at jc. Hmm.

But WAIT. What if the fault is not the fetch of jc but the fault the *hardware reports for the descriptor writeback*? Or... hmm.

Hold on, let me reconsider something fundamental: what if these "faults" are not real faults at all, but **the MMU reporting the *page-table walk* for the AS's own page tables**... no.

Alternatively: maybe the fault address == jc because **the JM's fetch is performed with the AS set but the address the MMU sees is the *physical* jc** (which the CPU-side walk matched) — no.

OK here's another thought, and I think it's important: in Midgard, when a job's descriptor is fetched, the JM *writes back* to the descriptor (words 0..3: exception_status, first_incomplete_task, fault_pointer). That's a WRITE. If the descriptor page were mapped read-only, you'd get a permission fault (0xC8), not 0xD8.

Hmm, what about the "ACCESS_FLAG" semantic in these GPU MMUs: maybe it's raised when the hardware performs an *atomic/exclusive* access or a "clean" operation and the ATE's attribute doesn't permit... no.

Let me step back and consider that 0xD8 might not be AF at all, but Midgard's code for **"fault on an ATE that is 'valid' but whose walk hit the 'access flag' update path"** — i.e. the MMU hardware *wants to set AF* on the ATE and something blocks it. If the MMU hardware maintains AF by writing to the ATE, and the ATE's page (page table) is... fine.

Alternatively 0xD8's real meaning could be "the address was translated but the *page table entry's access-flag/TLB state* requires a retry" = a *spurious/retry* fault. kbase lumps it as a name only; if it's retryable, that explains why 3 faults occur but the job usually completes: the MMU retries and succeeds.

So the practical statement: the 0x800002d8 descriptor-class faults are **non-fatal, retryable events** (the job proceeds; NODRAW run has one and no timeout), and the 0x810002d8 data-class faults are also non-fatal (the job completes). The timeout (0x08) happens on 1/8 runs *without* a corresponding new fault class. That means the ACCESS_FLAG faults are probably **noise** (a hardware/MMU retry artifact on this part), and the real hang cause is something else entirely!

Hmm, that reframes everything. The peer's earlier claim "1 of 4 timed out" and "7/8 descriptor faults but 1/8 timeouts" → faults happen almost every run, timeouts rarely. So faults ≠ hang.

So what causes the 1/8 hang? Something intermittent with the same "no DONE/ERR, ACTIVE 0x08" signature. Candidates from my kbase comparison:
- The job is blocked on a memory transaction (but we now see the MMU faults are retryable and probably not it).
- The tiler/fragment job genuinely waiting on tile lists (the producer/consumer handshake) — e.g. the fragment job dispatched before the tiler job completed (ordering), which the port tries to guarantee via serial_prev + the fragment's own deps.
- Recovery-side: the hang could be a *lost DONE* after all — but rawstat=0 rules that out.

Hmm. Since faults are constant and timeouts are rare, the discriminating question is: what differs in the timeout runs? The peer says in the timed-out run, the ring showed only data faults (no descriptor line) and the TIMEOUT-DIAG FAULTADDRESS was the jc (0x299a55c0) — but the ring (EVRING) is budget-bounded so maybe incomplete.

Given the impossibility of resolving it from here, the highest-value reply is:

(a) Answer the map-print question definitively: the print is behind a *shared* 64-line global budget (`p7580_iova_trace` at submit.c:150), decremented by BOTH unmap (:955) and map (:1305); also `p7580_drv_map_bo` returns early with no print when the BO is already in `drv->bo_list` (:1216-1220), and the entry is added once and removed only at GEM free (gem.c:1188-1204). So: (i) each BO is mapped exactly once in its lifetime; (ii) zero "map" lines means the budget was consumed by unmap lines or earlier maps — check "p7580_iova: unmap". Consequence for their correlation plan: a map-time correlation is impossible after 64 events; they must change the print (e.g. `pr_info` unconditionally for the next build, or use a static counter with a much bigger budget) or add an ioctl/debugfs query.

(b) The really useful structural consequence of the early-return: **a BO is mapped once, at its first submit, and never again.** So a stale-TLB theory for a *page that was mapped long ago* is much less likely, and the "map happens right before dispatch" race window only exists for a BO's *first ever* use. In particular: all BOs in a batch are typically fresh → the race window is exactly at first use → still consistent.

(c) The dominant new fact: faults are near-universal (7/8 runs, and even NODRAW always) while the timeout is 1/8 → **the ACCESS_FLAG faults cannot be the hang trigger**. Retract that causal link explicitly (I said earlier "one root cause covers both"): the faults are a separate, retryable artifact. The hang needs its own cause, and my ranked analysis should be re-ranked:
   - The jc-fetch-class fault coincides with the jc address — but since it happens in 7/8 runs without a hang, it's not sufficient.
   - So the 0x08 stall's cause has to be found by *differencing* a hanging run from a non-hanging run.

(d) Give them the differential diagnostics that would separate a hang from a non-hang cheaply — this is where the port's existing instrumentation helps:
   1. On every TIMEOUT, dump the *other* slot's state too (JS_COMMAND_NEXT, JS_STATUS, HEAD/TAIL for slot 1) and the tiler/polygon-list SFBD fields (heap_start/heap_end/pl/pl_body). A hang caused by "fragment waiting for tiles" shows a complete chain and empty/partial polygon list; a hang caused by "descriptor never fetched" shows... the same ACTIVE.
   2. Add the `JSn_COMMAND`/`JS_STATUS` pair *right after START* (they already do post-start), plus a periodic (100 ms) JS_STATUS/HEAD sample during the timeout window — that distinguishes "never progressed past fetch" (HEAD==TAIL==jc forever, no MMU activity) from "running but stalled mid-frame".
   3. The decisive one: **check whether the *tiler* ever produced the polygon list** — the port already dumps the SFBD page; add a dump of the polygon list header (pl, 1024×8 B) at timeout and compare with a successful run.
   4. And bit-24 discriminator + per-fault timestamps so they can prove the fault set is identical between hang/no-hang runs (which would prove the faults are innocent).

(e) Also give them the kbase-canonical resolution path for a *stalled* slot that does NOT depend on knowing why: HARD_STOP via JSn_COMMAND (0x20) not COMMAND_NEXT (0x60) — job.c:1486 vs mali_kbase_jm.c:553/694-706. Their recovery currently writes COMMAND_NEXT, which for a job that is *current* does nothing; yet their recovery "works" (recover-done drain_rc=0, slot idle) because the GPU soft reset clears it. So the reset is doing the work — meaning recovery is heavier than needed and destroys the evidence. Recommend: before the reset, try JSn_COMMAND=HARD_STOP and log whether JS_STATUS leaves 0x08. That both fixes recovery and, if JS_STATUS *doesn't* leave 0x08, proves the block is wedged at fabric level.

(f) On the 3 data faults at the allocator top: now that the pad experiment shows the cluster *moves* with the top of the allocation space (0x29654000 → 0x39a5f000 when a separate-fd pad BO is added... wait, they said the pad opened its own DRM fd so IOVAs are per-file; the cluster moved to 0x39a5f000 — meaning the cluster tracks the top of *that file's* space). So the reader's address is a function of the allocator cursor, not of any buffer → strongly suggests the address is **a BO IOVA that was carved out but whose BO is not (yet) mapped**, i.e. "read at the IOVA of the next allocation". Since the port assigns IOVAs at CREATE and maps at first submit, a BO created *but used before its first submit* gives exactly this. Userspace-visible: Mesa creates the BO and submits it in the same batch normally... but a BO referenced *only through a pointer inside another BO* (e.g. a descriptor pointing at a pool sub-allocation in a DIFFERENT BO) may never be in bo_handles → never mapped → reads at its IOVA fault forever. But then the fault would be persistent, not "3 loads then done"... consistent! The GPU gives up after 3 loads (drops the draw data) and completes.

So (f) proposal: **find the BO whose IOVA == the fault address.** They can do this from userspace! `drm_panfrost_create_bo` returns `offset` = the IOVA. So: log every CREATE_BO offset+size from Mesa (LD_PRELOAD or the diag patch's bo create print already exists) and check whether any BO in the process has offset == fault address. If YES → the BO exists, is never mapped by the kernel (not in bo_handles) → exact root cause and a kernel fix: map at create/mmap like kbase, or map every BO in the process at submit time.

That's a crisp, userspace-only decisive test they can run right now (they already have the jh/diag hooks that print bo create). Excellent — I'll lead with that.

Wait — but the peer said earlier "Attribution in the earlier 64x64 draw run: both faulting ranges are NOT inside any BO of that process". Hmm, so they already checked ERR-MAP-based attribution... but ERR-MAP only lists *submitted* BOs. They need the CREATE_BO log (all BOs). If the fault address matches a CREATE_BO offset, mystery solved. Their statement "not inside any BO of that process" may have been based on ERR-MAP. So I should ask precisely for that: compare against the full CREATE_BO list (offset field returned by the ioctl), not ERR-MAP.

Also note the Mesa pool: `TRANSIENT_SLAB_SIZE` and the observation "last-BO size observed was 0x9000" — 0x9000 = 36KB. Hmm, and the fault cluster is at the top of the allocation space.

So the plan for the reply:
1. Explain the missing map print (shared 64-budget; early return for already-linked BOs; map happens once per BO lifetime). Tell them to grep "p7580_iova: unmap" and to bump the trace for the next build; correlation as planned is impossible.
2. Retract my "one root cause" claim: faults are near-universal (NODRAW always faults; 7/8 draw runs fault) while timeouts are 1/8 → the ACCESS_FLAG faults are a retryable artifact, not the hang trigger. The hang needs a differential diagnosis.
3. Decisive userspace test for the data cluster: compare the fault VA against the full CREATE_BO offset list (not ERR-MAP). If a BO with offset == fault VA exists, it was never mapped (not in any bo_handles) → that's the bug and the fix is kbase-style mapping at create/mmap.
4. For the hang: recovery should try JSn_COMMAND=HARD_STOP before resetting (kbase mali_kbase_jm.c:553, 694-706 vs our job.c:1486 COMMAND_NEXT) — and log whether JS_STATUS leaves 0x08. Plus a periodic 100 ms sample of JS_STATUS/HEAD/TAIL during the hang window to distinguish "fetch never happened" from "running and stalled", plus slot-1 state and the polygon-list dump at timeout.
5. Also mention: the NODRAW single fault at 0x2961e280 — is that address the *chain jc* of that submit? If yes, the pattern "fault address == jc of the job we just dispatched" holds even for a clear job, and then the interesting question is whether the *first* JOB fetch of every submit faults once and retries. That would make it a per-dispatch event = suspicious of the START sequence/config rather than of page tables (e.g. START_MMU vs the AS enable timing!). Hmm!! That's worth flagging:

**If every dispatch produces exactly one ACCESS_FLAG fault at its own jc and then retries successfully, the cause is the job fetch racing the AS/mapping state** — e.g. `JSn_CONFIG_START_MMU` set means "start the MMU for this job" (issue 10649 workaround) and the first fetch happens while the MMU is coming up. kbase sets START_MMU too... but kbase also does an explicit MMU enable/`kbase_mmu_update` before submitting.

Ask them to check: does the single NODRAW fault address equal *that submit's* jc? If yes, it's a per-dispatch event, and the next question is whether it also happens when the same submit is dispatched twice (same BO, already-mapped) — the "second identical submit" test would show whether it's a first-fetch artifact or a per-write artifact. That's a great cheap test: dispatch the *same* chain twice back-to-back and count faults (1 vs 2).

That "same descriptor dispatched twice" test is very clean: if the SECOND dispatch of the identical jc does not fault, it's a first-touch/TLB-fill artifact; if it faults again, it's per-dispatch (config/AS-timing).

Good. Let me write this up concisely. Also correct my earlier over-claim explicitly (intellectual honesty, and it matters for their debugging).

Length: aim ~500 words.

arguments.content:
Three answers, one correction, one cheap decisive test.

1) Why `p7580_iova: map` never appears — code, not mystery. The print is behind a SHARED 64-line global budget: `unsigned int p7580_iova_trace = 64;` at submit.c:150, decremented by BOTH the unmap print (submit.c:955-957, "p7580_iova: unmap ...") and the map print (submit.c:1305-1309). Grep "p7580_iova: unmap": if those lines exist, the budget was spent by frees before your draw. Also `p7580_drv_map_bo` returns 0 with NO print when the object is already in drv->bo_list (submit.c:1212-1220), and that entry is added once and removed only at GEM free (gem.c:1188-1204, p7580_gem_gpu_unmap). So a BO is mapped exactly once in its whole lifetime, at its first submit. Your filter never leaks: it is guarded by pr_info budget only, but the budget is burned by unmaps too. For the correlation you want, make that print unconditional for one build (or a debugfs counter of {iova,size,npages,ktime} per map) — otherwise you get 64 events per boot, all at the start.

2) CORRECTION to what I told you earlier: faults are not the hang. Your own numbers kill my "one root cause" claim — NODRAW faults in 2/2 runs with zero timeouts, draw faults in 7/8 with 1/8 timeouts. So 0x810002d8 / 0x800002d8 are a *retryable* artifact of this MMU (the transaction is replayed; the job pays nothing), and the 0x08 stall has a separate, intermittent trigger. Drop the fault→hang link from the diagnosis; keep the bit-24 tag only for identification. Sorry for the extra lap.

3) The one test I would run next, and it is userspace-only. I now believe the 3-load cluster is an access to a BO that the kernel never mapped, and you can prove or kill it without a flash: drm_panfrost_create_bo returns `offset` = the IOVA (our ioctl sets it, panfrost7580_ioctl.c:246-249). Log every CREATE_BO {offset,size} in the process (your diag hook already prints bo create) and compare the fault VAs (0x29654000/f100/f200, and 0x39a5f000-family in the pad run) against the FULL create list. ERR-MAP cannot answer this: it lists only the BOs of that submit's bo_handles. If a BO exists with offset == fault VA (or offset <= VA < offset+size), the GPU is reading a live BO that our driver never gave leaves to, because mapping here is submit-driven and only for handle-listed BOs (submit.c:1208-1290 from the loop at :1841-1862); kbase maps at mmap/alloc time, kbase_gpu_mmap. Fix would be kbase-style: map on create/mmap, not on first submit. If instead no BO owns that VA, the reader is addressing past the allocator cursor and it is a plain over-read in the consumer.

4) For the actual hang, two cheap things that produce knowledge either way:
  a. In recovery, before the reset, write HARD_STOP to the CURRENT command register (JSn_COMMAND, offset 0x20) instead of JS_COMMAND_NEXT (0x60) — panfrost7580_job.c:1486 does the latter, kbase stops a running job with JSn_COMMAND only after checking COMMAND_NEXT == 0 (mali_kbase_jm.c:553 with the eviction logic at :694-706). Print JSn_STATUS immediately after. If it leaves 0x08 -> you just fixed recovery *and* proved the JM can still be steered; if it stays 0x08 -> the block is wedged at fabric level and only the reset/power-cycle clears it, which is what your recovery is actually doing today (masking the evidence).
  b. During the ~750 ms window sample JSn_STATUS/HEAD/TAIL (and slot 1's, plus the polygon-list head) every 100 ms. "HEAD==TAIL==jc from the first sample, nothing ever changes" (fetch never completed) and "HEAD moves / status changes then freezes" (execution stalled mid-frame) are different bugs, and that log tells them apart for the price of a timer.

5) One question worth one run, because it decides whether the single descriptor-class fault is per-dispatch or per-first-touch: does the NODRAW fault address equal that submit's own jc? And then dispatch the identically-same chain twice back-to-back — 1 fault vs 2 faults. One fault for two identical dispatches => first-touch TLB/AS-start artifact (and then JSn_CONFIG_START_MMU timing is the suspect); a fault on each dispatch => it is per-START, i.e. the fetch races the AS, which is a much more actionable finding than page-table content.

arguments.content:
Your DRAWS=2 outlier is the best datum either of us has produced: 2 dispatches, 1 desc fault, and that is the run that timed out. That settles the causality — the ACCESS_FLAG event is not a fault to fix but the *retry handshake*: delivered => the fetch is replayed and nobody notices; not delivered => the fetch never replays and the slot sits ACTIVE with HEAD latched. So stop looking at page-table content (your per-START/per-dispatch data already killed it) and treat this as "a START whose first fetch got no handshake".

Two experiments, both on SMOKE_DRAWS=2:

A) Targeted flush on timeout, BEFORE the reset — this is the one that can convert the stall into progress and prove the mechanism. In p7580_job_recover(), before the GPU reset, do exactly what the map path does for one page: p7580_mmu_invalidate(regs, 0, jc >> PAGE_SHIFT, 1, 1) then poll JSn_STATUS for ~10 ms and log it. If JS_STATUS leaves 0x08 (or the fence signals right after), the fetch was blocked waiting for a translation event and a flush rescues it — permanent fix then is "flush the jc range on every START, or right after the first fault". If it stays 0x08, the fetch is wedged below the MMU and only the reset/power-cycle clears it.

B) Stop the CURRENT job, not the next one — panfrost7580_job.c:1486 writes HARD_STOP to JS_COMMAND_NEXT (0x60), which for a job that is already current is a no-op (kbase only NOPs COMMAND_NEXT when it is non-zero, then stops the current job via JSn_COMMAND 0x20: mali_kbase_jm.c:694-706 and the actual write at :553). Change it to P7580_JS_COMMAND (0x20) and log JSn_STATUS immediately after writes. Leaves 0x08 => genuinely wedged (B is then only a latency win); goes 0x03/0x04 => your recovery stops destroying state, and the "tiler did not idle, aborting suspend" cascade should stop too.

C) While you are in the MMU handler, close a real lost-event window, kbase-style. Ours reads MMU_INT_STAT once and then writes the whole word to MMU_INT_CLEAR (panfrost7580_main.c:85-117) with MASK left at 0xFFFFFFFF, so an event that latches between the read and the clear on the same bit is erased. kbase saves the mask, writes MMU_IRQ_MASK=0, clears only the handled AS's bit, and restores a mask with the handled ASes removed, then re-enables per AS in mmu_mask_reenable (mali_kbase_mmu.c:1109-1117, :1147+, :1205-1210, :95-107). Minimal version for us: save rawstat, MASK=0, handle AS0, CLEAR=1<<0 (and 1<<16), then MASK=0xFFFFFFFF, then re-read STAT and loop until 0. Expected effect: hang rate drops on SMOKE_DRAWS=2 if event loss contributed; no change if the event genuinely never fires. Either answer is worth the 6 lines.

On the data cluster, one shape hint now that you have three of them: 3-4 loads at 0x100 stride = a ~0x300-0x400 read, and 0x400 is exactly one 16x16 RGBA8 tile, so "one tile past the last tile" is the geometry to check. To identify the pointer without new code, compare each cluster base against the values you already dump: SFBD +0xC8 (polygon_list), +0xD0 (pl_body), +0xD8/+0xE0 (heap_start/heap_end), the renderer-state TLS/attribute bases, and every chain node's payload words. If one of those equals the cluster base, you have the field; if none does, it is a pure consumer over-read with the cursor as base. It never hangs, so keep it out of the hang workstream.

For the record, 0x08 = ACTIVE is now vendor-confirmed twice: BASE_JD_EVENT_ACTIVE = 0x08, mali_base_kernel.h:751, and kbase_exception_name case 0x08 "ACTIVE", mali_kbase_mmu.c:1233-1235.

<irc>
Incoming IRC message from agent `Mesa203Build`:

New capture (SMOKE_DRAWS=2, hang on attempt 1) changes two things. Both are your call, but here is the raw material.

A) The "timeouts" I counted in my 8-run sample are NOT the KWin stall. In this capture the three timeouts are slot=1 with
  p7580_job: TIMEOUT slot=1 js_status=0x00000000 (NOT_STARTED/OK) stat=0x2 rawstat=0x2 head=0x29654000 tail=0x29654000 seq=0 jc_age=0
and seq=1 (jc=0x29654100), seq=2 (jc=0x29654200), each followed by post-reset + recover-done latched=0x00000000. So: js_status 0x00/head==tail, not 0x08 ACTIVE, latched=0. My earlier "1 in 8 runs hangs like KWin" claim was wrong — it conflates a NOT_STARTED slot timeout with the ACTIVE stall. Discount those 1/8 and 3-in-4 numbers; the ACTIVE (0x08) stall I have only from the 64x64 draw runs and the 720x1280 run, and only there is latched=0x8.

B) The 3 addresses at 0x100 stride are not past-a-BO over-reads of data — they are THREE CHAINED TILER JOB DESCRIPTORS, and they live in the one-page hole between two BOs of this process. This run's own create list:
  h12 size=0x10000 iova=0x29644000..0x29654000
  h13 size=0x10000 iova=0x29655000..0x29665000      <- allocator skipped 0x29654000..0x29655000
and the driver's own JDBODY dump reads plausible descriptors at exactly those addresses:
  JDBODY slot=1 seq=0 jc=0x29654000  ... 00010005 ... 29644000 ...
  JDBODY slot=1 seq=1 jc=0x29654100  ... 0002000b ... 2961e390 ... 2961e370 ... 29631000 ... 2961e320 2961e350 2961e2e0 2961e2c0 2961e180
  JDBODY slot=1 seq=2 jc=0x29654200  ... 0003000f ... 29632040 ... 2961e420 ... 2961e3c0 ... 2961e400 3f800000
Header words 00010005 / 0002000b / 0003000f are a clean 3-node chain (low half = node index, high half = type/size), and the payload pointers are all real Mesa BO addresses of this process (0x2961e1xx family = the 64 KiB pool at h5). So the page at 0x29654000 IS mapped and contains a valid chain, yet no BO of this process owns it — the only way I can see that happening is stale AS0 page-table leaves (and stale physical content) surviving the previous DRM file's close, at an IOVA the bump allocator reuses; the 1-page guard between BOs makes exactly that page visible at the boundary.

Two things worth your instrumentation: (1) whether map_bo's "already in drv->bo_list" short-circuit (submit.c:1212-1220) also skips the leaf insert when the *page tables* were reset/reused; (2) whether file close/program_as ever clears AS0 leaves — if it does, the JDBODY read at 0x29654000 should have returned zeros and it did not.

Nothing further from me: the 20.3.5 stack is unchanged and verified (GL_RENDERER/GL_VERSION PASS, eglSwapBuffers ok), and these captures are on disk at /data/mesa203-build/dm-d2-*.txt plus /data/mesa203-build/dm-pad*.txt if you want them.

And the port's TIMEOUT line prints stat/rawstat — so at timeout, the DONE bit for slot 1 was SET but the fence wasn't signaled?! Wait, if the IRQ handler had demuxed it, the fence would signal. stat=0x2 at timeout means the DONE bit is latched but *nobody cleared/handled it* — or the handler ran and cleared then a new one latched...

arguments.content:
Both of your candidate explanations are ruled out by the code, and the datum you captured points at a third one that the log can prove.

1) "Partial rewrite / a node still carries an original-page pointer": impossible. p7580_chain_hdr_isolate zeroes everything that can lead anywhere — w[5]=0 (both deps), w[6]=0, w[7]=0 (next lo/hi), and only rewrites the index field (jm_hw.h:419-425). A shadow node is a standalone descriptor with next=0, so a JM started on it cannot walk into the original page or anywhere else. Also no slot overlap: job_bytes caps at 192 (VERTEX/TILER/FUSED), 56 (WRITE_VALUE), 64 (FRAGMENT) — jm_hw.h:362-378 — all < the 256 stride, so no node's payload can spill into the next slot.

2) "HEAD latches the pre-rewrite JC while the fetch uses the rewritten one": not a contradiction — those are two different jobs. 0x2243a5c0 sits in the original pool page, which is what the *fragment* submit dispatches: a 1-node, zero-dep descriptor takes the standalone path (need_shadow = nodes>1 || dep1 || dep2 || stale words, submit.c:1949-1966), so it is never shadowed and its HEAD/TAIL legitimately reads the Mesa page. Meanwhile the 14 faults are slot 1's chain reading shadow 0x22470000 (the chain print proves that submit took the shadow branch). You are comparing slot 0's job with slot 1's fetches. Please dump HEAD/TAIL/JS_STATUS/COMMAND_NEXT for BOTH slots at timeout — the TIMEOUT line only prints the timed-out slot.

3) The real reading of 0x22470240: node 2's slot starts at 0x22470200 and a VERTEX/TILER descriptor is 192 bytes, so +0x240 is offset 0x40 inside node 2 — the Draw block. A translation fault is page-granular: the MMU cannot fault at +0x240 while having served +0x200/+0x220 in the same page. Therefore the page WAS mapped when the JM read node 2's header and was UNMAPPED before it read the Draw word. That is p7580_drv_shadow_put() running while the GPU still had an outstanding fetch: the last node's ref drops -> p7580_gem_gpu_unmap(sh->obj) -> leaves cleared -> the JM retries forever (your 14 identical faults) and the slot never retires. Which is the same disease as (A): the port retires/frees a job the hardware has not finished with.

How to prove it in one build, two ways:
 a) Log the shadow's lifetime: print in p7580_drv_shadow_put the shadow IOVA, atomic_read(&sh->refs) before the dec and whether this call is the last one (submit.c:1506-1520), and grep your capture for 'iova=0x22470000' unmap ordered against the 14 faults. If the unmap precedes them, it is proven.
 b) One-line experiment: comment out the p7580_gem_gpu_unmap() call in p7580_drv_shadow_put (leak the mapping and the IOVA for the test). If the 14 faults and the 0x08 stall disappear, early unmap is confirmed as the mechanism; if they persist, the page was never mapped and the suspect becomes the create path instead (p7580_drv_map_bo returning 0 silently for a fresh object cannot happen — it only short-circuits on an existing drv->bo_list entry, submit.c:1212-1220 — so a never-mapped shadow would have to be a map_bo failure being ignored).

Note what this implies for the fix, and it is kbase's actual discipline: kbase never releases a VA region while a job that can still touch it is on the GPU — the atom holds the region reference and the region is only freed after the job is guaranteed gone (and after a hard-stop plus GPU reset if it is not). Our shadow has per-node refs (atomic_set(&sh->refs, nodes), submit.c:1479), so it is freed by whichever node retires last — which is only correct if retire order equals hardware order. With one-job-per-DONE-bit retirement and no JOB_IRQ_JS_STATE accounting, that assumption is exactly what breaks.

Also: the ACCESS_FLAG family vanishing in #42 and being replaced by 100% translation faults is consistent with this — you changed which failure mode dominates, not the underlying lifetime bug. And your (A) state (DONE latched, stat/rawstat=0x2, js 0x00) is still a separate observation worth fixing on its own.

On the readback request: post-start/irq-arm are budget-gated (trace_left), so no value from this capture — the shadow_put/unmap ordering above is the better instrument anyway.
